items.food_name: Maize stiff porridge (nsima), whole maize flour
items.method: non-ISO (11 healthy adult volunteers, glucose reference, 3-week protocol)
items.source: Mlotha V, et al. 2016. "Glycemic responses to maize flour stiff porridges prepared using local recipes in Malawi." Food Science & Nutrition. DOI: 10.1002/fsn3.293
items.notes: Traditional whole-maize-flour nsima as consumed in Malawi. High GI attributed to traditional processing, preparation, and cooking methods.

items.method: non-ISO (11 healthy adult volunteers, glucose reference, 3-week protocol)
items.source: Mlotha V, et al. 2016. "Glycemic responses to maize flour stiff porridges prepared using local recipes in Malawi." Food Science & Nutrition. DOI: 10.1002/fsn3.293
items.notes: GI above the 100 glucose reference is possible with this test-food methodology and is reported as-is in the source; treat as 'very high' rather than a literal >100% comparison.

items.food_name: Maize stiff porridge (nsima), fermented maize grits
items.method: non-ISO (11 healthy adult volunteers, glucose reference, 3-week protocol)
items.source: Mlotha V, et al. 2016. "Glycemic responses to maize flour stiff porridges prepared using local recipes in Malawi." Food Science & Nutrition. DOI: 10.1002/fsn3.293
items.notes: Lowest-GI nsima variant tested — fermentation before milling into grits moderated the glycaemic response relative to whole-flour or unfermented-grits nsima.

items.source: Atkinson FS, Brand-Miller JC, Foster-Powell K, Buyken AE, Goletzke J. 2021. "International tables of glycemic index and glycemic load values 2021: a systematic review." Am J Clin Nutr 114(5):1625-1632.
items.notes: 73±4 is the ISO-standard point estimate; wide variety/region-dependent range (65-94) is well documented — jasmine and short-grain varieties trend higher, basmati and parboiled trend lower.

items.source: Atkinson FS, Brand-Miller JC, Foster-Powell K, Buyken AE, Goletzke J. 2021. "International tables of glycemic index and glycemic load values 2021: a systematic review." Am J Clin Nutr 114(5):1625-1632.
items.notes: 68±4. Consistently lower than white rice across studies, attributed to intact bran/fiber slowing starch digestion.

items.source: Foster-Powell K, Holt SH, Brand-Miller JC. 2002. "International table of glycemic index and glycemic load values." Am J Clin Nutr 76(1):5-56; updated in Atkinson et al. 2021 (as above).
items.notes: Potato GI varies widely by variety, cooking method, and whether served hot or cooled (cooked-and-cooled potato can drop to ~49 due to resistant starch formation).

items.source: Atkinson FS, Brand-Miller JC, Foster-Powell K, Buyken AE, Goletzke J. 2021. "International tables of glycemic index and glycemic load values 2021: a systematic review." Am J Clin Nutr 114(5):1625-1632.
items.notes: Mashing/instant preparation raises GI further versus plain boiled — instant mashed potato averages higher still (~84).

items.source: Foster-Powell K, Holt SH, Brand-Miller JC. 2002. "International table of glycemic index and glycemic load values." Am J Clin Nutr 76(1):5-56; updated in Atkinson et al. 2021 (as above).
items.notes: Cooking method matters a lot here: baked or roasted sweet potato is reported considerably higher (~86-88) than boiled.

items.method: mixed — ISO and non-ISO studies pooled
items.source: International Tables of Glycemic Index Values (as compiled in Atkinson et al. 2021); British Journal of Nutrition (cassava, peeled/boiled/frozen/thawed/reheated, 94±11); regional study reporting boiled cassava with salt (Kenya) at 46.
items.notes: No Malawi-specific cassava GI study found. Published values swing from low to very high depending on variety, cooking method, and whether the sample was frozen/reheated — treat any single number for cassava with real caution until a Malawi/regional study exists.
